SC suspends Godhra train burning convict’s life term on medical grounds days after bail to Bilkis’ rapists

Irfan Siraj Pada, one of the 31 convicts in the case, sought relief on two grounds—to treat his heart ailment, and his 18-year long incarceration.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the life sentence of one of the convicts of the 2002 Godhra train burning case, taking in consideration his heart ailment and his 18-year long incarceration. Irfan Siraj Pada was arrested in 2002 and was among the 31 convicted by a special court in 2011 in the 27 February 2002 Sabarmati Express burning incident which left 58 people dead and led to communal riots in Gujarat.

A bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale granted bail to Pada and noted that his application was filed primarily on medical grounds and the Gujarat government had submitted that his condition—as stated by him—has been established as factually correct.

Pada had sought suspension of his life sentence and release on bail strictly on medical grounds while his appeal against conviction remained pending. His plea sought temporary relief on two primary grounds—to manage and receive treatment for his cardiovascular disease, and the fact that he had spent 18 years in prison while awaiting the final hearing of his 2018 appeal.

Show Full Article

In this case, his counsel explicitly clarified before the bench that the plea argued solely on humanitarian and health grounds, not on the merits of his conviction.

Advocate Swati Ghildiyal, appearing for the Gujarat government also told the court that she had no objection to the suspension of sentence on medical grounds.

This report will be updated when the order copy is released.

Notably, this order comes almost a month after the same bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale granted bail to two convicts sentenced to life imprisonment in the Bilkis Bano case. The bench had suspended their sentence while noting they had spent more than 17 years in prison and one of them was handicapped.

Also Read: The relentless Bilkis Bano: All the times she turned to the courts to fight back

Case history A special court in Ahmedabad had convicted Pada and 30 others in the case in 2011, nine years after the train burning incident. Of the 31, 11 were sentenced to death and the remaining 20 were sentenced to life imprisonment while 63 other accused were acquitted.

Six years later in 2017, the Gujarat High Court commuted the 11 death sentences to life sentences and upheld the life sentences for the other 20. Their appeal remains pending before the top court since 2018.

In 2020, the Indian Express reported that two weeks after Gujarat BJP councillor Hiren Patel was killed while out on a morning walk, police arrested four persons for allegedly executing the contract killing.

Among the four accused was Pada, who had been on the run since jumping parole in 2019. In November 2024, a Dahod sessions court acquitted Pada and all eight other accused in the murder case, giving them the benefit of the doubt. Despite his acquittal in the murder case, Pada remained in jail to serve his existing life sentence in the 2002 Godhra train burning case.

In April 2025, a Supreme Court bench comprising Justices A.S. Oka (now retired) and U. Bhuyan granted him interim parole while the Gujarat government considered his plea for premature release.

He was also granted parole by the high court to attend his brother’s wedding and again in February this year to attend his grandmother’s funeral.

(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)

Gandhi dynasty’s past a bestseller, but political future of Congress remains uncertain—The Economist

The Financial Times examines a brewing dispute over commission caps in the insurance sector & a Reuters report featured in The Guardian looks at Congress’s confrontation with Meta.

Prakhar Agarwal

23 November, 2026 03:13 pm IST

New Delhi: The questions surrounding India’s political future, economic ambitions and freedom of expression continue to draw attention from the international media. In its latest Asia column, The Economist takes a look at the Gandhi family’s political legacy, drawing on Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, ‘Belonging: A Journey of Love’.

Titled ‘ The Gandhi dynasty suffers for India — And India suffers the Gandhi dynasty ’, the article weighs in on Gandhi family’s claim to have protected India’s secular and democratic values. It opens with a pointed remark: “THANK GOODNESS for the Gandhi family. If it weren’t for them, India might have fallen into the grip of Hindu nationalists bent on destroying the country’s secular foundations and eradicating its diversity.”

The magazine revisits former prime minister Indira Gandhi’s decision to impose the Emergency in 1975, when she feared that her political opponents would “destroy the country” and that the Congress would “split and scatter”. The irony, the article notes, was that her attempt to protect the country involved suspending civil liberties, censoring the press and jailing opposition leaders.

Show Full Article

It then turns to Rajiv Gandhi, who entered politics out of “the pull of duty towards his mother [and] his country”. But the magazine points to his government’s record, including the anti-Sikh pogrom following Indira’s assassination, for which it says “his affable manner did not absolve” him of “moral responsibility”.

Sonia Gandhi’s own account of entering politics is also examined. Despite describing the political world as one of “ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery”, she repeatedly presents her role in the Congress as a matter of duty. The magazine contrasts this with the corruption allegations that dogged the Manmohan Singh government, noting that “integrity was not a word often used for his government”.

The article ends with the next generation of the family: Rahul Gandhi as Leader of the Opposition and Priyanka Gandhi as a lawmaker, while Narendra Modi is in “his third term as prime minister. Thank goodness, he must think, for the Gandhis.”

In The World in Brief, The Economist highlights the contrast between the success of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir and the declining political fortunes of her party. The book, which chronicles the Nehru-Gandhi family, sold 200,000 copies in its first week, making it “India’s fastest-selling book, according to HarperCollins,”

But, as the magazine puts it, “Much less can be said of the dynasty’s political fortunes.” The Gandhi family, which governed India for decades, since 2014. The piece captures this contrast in its closing line: “Ms Gandhi’s past may be a bestseller but Congress’s political future remains in doubt.”

Also Read: Women in public life to Adani’s business empire— Global Media on India’s growth story

F inancial Times writes India’s insurance brokers “are up in arms over a proposed cap on commissions, warning that it could hamper the growth of the country’s $126bn insurance sector,” even as the government looks to expand coverage and attract foreign investment.

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has proposed limiting commissions paid to brokers and agents to 2.5 percent for third-party motor insurance and up to 30 percent for term life policies. Currently, there are no such caps, and commissions can go as high as 81 percent for life insurance and 93 percent for health insurance.

The regulator wants to rein in these payouts to bring down costs for customers. But brokers argue that lower commissions could discourage agents from selling policies, particularly in areas where insurance penetration remains low.

“New business could dip during the transition,” Indian rating agency CareEdge said, warning that smaller insurers could face pressure to consolidate if the caps take effect in April.

The proposal comes as the government pursues its ‘Insurance for All by 2047’ target, under which it wants “every citizen” to have “adequate life, health and property insurance”. However, the regulator has pointed out that premium growth is not translating into a wider insured population. “This divergence indicates that premium growth is being driven more by higher-value sales to existing customers rather than by the expansion of the insured population,” it said.

Policybazaar chief executive Sarbvir Singh said lower commissions could hurt insurers as well as brokers: “If we don’t sell, then insurers will also have some impact.” Axis Max Life CFO Amrit Singh said the proposal had “pluses and minuses” and called for a “holistic” review.

The industry has also cautioned that regulatory uncertainty could deter investors. “If you are not becoming predictable, that will impact investment, and not just FDI,” an industry executive said, adding: “You cannot have this sword of changing regulations dangling.”

Also Read: Global media turns spotlight on Yogi Adityanath, says outcome of UP elections will ‘reverberate for years’

A Reuters report published by The Guardian looks at the growing confrontation between the Congress and Meta after Indian Youth Congress (IYC) members clashed with the police outside the company’s Hyderabad office over the removal of party leaders’ Instagram accounts. Two accounts were reinstated, but thousands belonging to journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.

Protests were also reported in Mumbai and in Gurugram as well. The demonstrations come amid a wider debate over online free speech and the “strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to”. In February, the government reduced the deadline for platforms to remove unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours. Reporters Without Borders says the “removal of journalistic content from social media has been on the rise in India this year”.

Meta has disclosed that it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, compared with around 70,000 in the whole of 2025. The company said most restrictions were made because it was “obligated to proactively restrict content” under local law requirements.

(Edited by Tony Rai)
